title: What does MECE mean, and how do you build a MECE structure?
description: What MECE means in plain English, how to test your own structure, and simple ways to make buckets that are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive.
hook: MECE is one of the first acronyms people meet in case prep, and one of the most confusing. It stands for mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive. In plain English: your buckets should not overlap, and together they should cover everything that matters. It sounds strict, but in practice it is a simple habit you can learn to check in a few seconds.
body:
Mutually exclusive: no overlap

Each idea should belong in only one bucket. If you split a retailer's problem into "online sales" and "young customers", you have a problem: young customers also shop online. Where would you put a 22-year-old buying online? Overlapping buckets lead to double counting and muddled conversations.

Collectively exhaustive: nothing big missing

Together, the buckets should cover the whole problem. If you split costs into "staff" and "rent", you have missed materials, energy, marketing and more. You do not need every tiny detail, but nothing important should be left out.

The easiest way to be MECE: use splits that add up

  • Maths splits: profit = revenue − costs; revenue = customers × spend per customer. These are MECE by definition.
  • Opposites: internal vs external, existing vs new, short term vs long term.
  • Steps in a process: order, pick, pack, deliver. Every part of the process sits in one step.
  • Segments: by region, product or customer type, as long as each customer fits in one segment.

A 10-second test

  1. Pick any idea. Does it fit in exactly one bucket? (Exclusive)
  2. Imagine the answer to the case. Would it fit in one of your buckets? (Exhaustive)

Do not let MECE freeze you

Interviewers do not expect a perfect structure. A structure that is 90% MECE and clearly tailored to the client beats a perfectly MECE one that could apply to any company. If you notice an overlap while presenting, just say so: "Actually, these two overlap a little; let me treat pricing only under revenue." That shows exactly the kind of thinking they want.

A non-overlapping split with a useful calculation

A retailer says sales are down 10%. Splitting the problem into "online", "young customers" and "London" is not mutually exclusive: one sale could belong to all three. Choose one dimension at a time. First, split sales into online and physical stores. Then split the channel causing the decline by customer segment or location.

Suppose physical stores fell from £8 million to £6 million, while online grew from £2 million to £3 million. Total revenue moved from £10 million to £9 million, so the decline is exactly £1 million or 10%. The £2 million store decline is partly offset by a £1 million online increase. You now know where to investigate: store traffic, store conversion and average transaction value.

MECE is a practical discipline, not a demand for perfect taxonomy under pressure. The structure should cover the major paths without double-counting, and it should lead to a next action. If the case is about a strategic choice rather than a numerical bridge, a clear sequence of distinct tests may be more useful than a rigid equation.
